# Post releases written without a dot, or without a number, are rejected

## What happens now

If a version ends with a post release, the word post has to be written with a
dot in front of it and a number after it. A version where the word post is
joined straight onto the release numbers, or where it is preceded by a dash,
or where no number follows the word, is turned down with an "Invalid version"
error. The same restriction applies when the post release appears inside a
requirement, so a rule that mentions such a post release is refused as well.

## What should happen

Every spelling people actually use for a post release should be accepted: the
word post attached to the numbers, the word post after a dot, the word post
after a dash, the word in capitals, and the word with no number after it at
all. When the number is left out, it should count as zero, and the version
should be shown back in the standard form with the dot and the number filled
in. Rules that mention a post release should accept the same spellings.

## About this project

This project is a small library for working with version numbers. It reads a
version that you give it, tells you whether the version is valid, sorts
versions, and checks a version against a requirement such as a minimum or an
exact match.

## Problem this solves

A lot of projects name their post releases without a dot before the word post,
with a dash instead, or with no number at all. Right now those real releases
cannot be read at all, so a project that uses such a name cannot be installed,
listed, or compared with others.

## What changed

Post releases are read in all the usual spellings instead of only the one
spelling with a dot and a number. A post release with no number is treated as
having a number of zero, and it is printed back with the dot and the number
added. Requirements that mention a post release accept the same spellings.
How versions are ordered against each other, and every other part of a version
such as the pre-release part, the development part and the local part, behave
exactly as before. Nothing was taken away.

## Impact

This is about compatibility and ease of use: version names that people
already use stop being rejected, and nothing that worked before changes.

## User experience

Before: I ask the library about a post release where the word post is joined
straight to the numbers, or written after a dash, and I get an "Invalid
version" error even though that name is used by a real project. After: the
same name is accepted, and when I print the version back I get the standard
form with the dot and, where the number was missing, a zero.

## Hints

- /workspace/packaging/version.py
- /workspace/tests/test_version.py
I'll start by reading the briefing, ticket, and hints files.

 370 │         return self.__class__(",".join([str(self), str(other)]))
 371 │ 
 372 │     def __eq__(self, other):
 373 │         if isinstance(other, string_types):
 374 │             other = Specifier(other)
 375 │         elif not isinstance(other, Specifier):
 376 │             return NotImplemented
 377 │ 
 378 │         return self._specs == other._specs
 379 │ 
 380 │     def __ne__(self, other):
 381 │         if isinstance(other, string_types):
 382 │             other = Specifier(other)
 383 │         elif not isinstance(other, Specifier):
 384 │             return NotImplemented
 385 │ 
 386 │         return self._specs != other._specs

 388 │     def __contains__(self, item):
 389 │         # Normalize item to a Version, this allows us to have a shortcut for
 390 │         # ``"2.0" in Specifier(">=2")
 391 │         version_item = item
 392 │         if not isinstance(item, Version):
 393 │             try:
 394 │                 version_item = Version(item)
 395 │             except ValueError:
 396 │                 # If we cannot parse this as a version, then we can only
 397 │                 # support identity comparison so do a quick check to see if the
 398 │                 # spec contains any non identity specifiers
 399 │                 #
 400 │                 # This will return False if we do not have any specifiers, this
 401 │                 # is on purpose as a non PEP 440 version should require
 402 │                 # explicit opt in because otherwise they cannot be sanely
 403 │                 # prioritized
 404 │                 if (not self._specs
 405 │                         or any(op != "===" for op, _ in self._specs)):
 406 │                     return False
 407 │ 
 408 │         # Ensure that the passed in version matches all of our version
 409 │         # specifiers
 410 │         return all(
 411 │             self._get_operator(op)(
 412 │                 version_item if op != "===" else item,
 413 │                 spec,
 414 │             )
 415 │             for op, spec, in self._specs
 416 │         )

 418 │     def _get_operator(self, op):
 419 │         return getattr(self, "_compare_{0}".format(self._operators[op]))
 420 │ 
 421 │     def _compare_compatible(self, prospective, spec):
 422 │         # Compatible releases have an equivalent combination of >= and ==. That
 423 │         # is that ~=2.2 is equivalent to >=2.2,==2.*. This allows us to
 424 │         # implement this in terms of the other specifiers instead of
 425 │         # implementing it ourselves. The only thing we need to do is construct
 426 │         # the other specifiers.
 427 │ 
 428 │         # We want everything but the last item in the version, but we want to
 429 │         # ignore post and dev releases and we want to treat the pre-release as
 430 │         # it's own separate segment.
 431 │         prefix = ".".join(
 432 │             list(
 433 │                 itertools.takewhile(
 434 │                     lambda x: (not x.startswith("post")
 435 │                                and not x.startswith("dev")),
 436 │                     _version_split(spec),
 437 │                 )
 438 │             )[:-1]
 439 │         )
 440 │ 
 441 │         # Add the prefix notation to the end of our string
 442 │         prefix += ".*"
 443 │ 
 444 │         return (self._get_operator(">=")(prospective, spec)
 445 │                 and self._get_operator("==")(prospective, prefix))
 446 │ 
 447 │     def _compare_equal(self, prospective, spec):
 448 │         # We need special logic to handle prefix matching
 449 │         if spec.endswith(".*"):
 450 │             # Split the spec out by dots, and pretend that there is an implicit
 451 │             # dot in between a release segment and a pre-release segment.
 452 │             spec = _version_split(spec[:-2])  # Remove the trailing .*
 453 │ 
 454 │             # Split the prospective version out by dots, and pretend that there
 455 │             # is an implicit dot in between a release segment and a pre-release
 456 │             # segment.
 457 │             prospective = _version_split(str(prospective))
 458 │ 
 459 │             # Shorten the prospective version to be the same length as the spec
 460 │             # so that we can determine if the specifier is a prefix of the
 461 │             # prospective version or not.
 462 │             prospective = prospective[:len(spec)]
 463 │ 
 464 │             # Pad out our two sides with zeros so that they both equal the same
 465 │             # length.
 466 │             spec, prospective = _pad_version(spec, prospective)
 467 │         else:
 468 │             # Convert our spec string into a Version
 469 │             spec = Version(spec)
 470 │ 
 471 │             # If the specifier does not have a local segment, then we want to
 472 │             # act as if the prospective version also does not have a local
 473 │             # segment.
 474 │             if not spec.local:
 475 │                 prospective = Version(prospective.public)

 477 │         return prospective == spec

 479 │     def _compare_not_equal(self, prospective, spec):
 480 │         return not self._compare_equal(prospective, spec)
 481 │ 
 482 │     def _compare_less_than_equal(self, prospective, spec):
 483 │         return prospective <= Version(spec)
 484 │ 
 485 │     def _compare_greater_than_equal(self, prospective, spec):
 486 │         return prospective >= Version(spec)
 487 │ 
 488 │     def _compare_less_than(self, prospective, spec):
 489 │         # Less than are defined as exclusive operators, this implies that
 490 │         # pre-releases do not match for the same series as the spec. This is
 491 │         # implemented by making <V imply !=V.*.
 492 │         return (prospective < Version(spec)
 493 │                 and self._get_operator("!=")(prospective, spec + ".*"))
 494 │ 
 495 │     def _compare_greater_than(self, prospective, spec):
 496 │         # Greater than are defined as exclusive operators, this implies that
 497 │         # pre-releases do not match for the same series as the spec. This is
 498 │         # implemented by making >V imply !=V.*.
 499 │         return (prospective > Version(spec)
 500 │                 and self._get_operator("!=")(prospective, spec + ".*"))
 501 │ 
 502 │     def _compare_identity(self, prospective, spec):
 503 │         return prospective.lower() == spec.lower()

 506 │ _prefix_regex = re.compile(r"^([0-9]+)((?:a|b|c|rc)[0-9]+)$")
 507 │

 509 │ def _version_split(version):
 510 │     result = []
 511 │     for item in version.split("."):
 512 │         match = _prefix_regex.search(item)
 513 │         if match:
 514 │             result.extend(match.groups())
 515 │         else:
 516 │             result.append(item)
 517 │     return result

 519 │ 
 520 │ def _pad_version(left, right):
 521 │     left_split, right_split = [], []
 522 │ 
 523 │     # Get the release segment of our versions
 524 │     left_split.append(list(itertools.takewhile(lambda x: x.isdigit(), left)))
 525 │     right_split.append(list(itertools.takewhile(lambda x: x.isdigit(), right)))
 526 │ 
 527 │     # Get the rest of our versions
 528 │     left_split.append(left[len(left_split):])
 529 │     right_split.append(left[len(right_split):])
 530 │ 
 531 │     # Insert our padding
 532 │     left_split.insert(
 533 │         1,
 534 │         ["0"] * max(0, len(right_split[0]) - len(left_split[0])),
 535 │     )
 536 │     right_split.insert(
 537 │         1,
 538 │         ["0"] * max(0, len(left_split[0]) - len(right_split[0])),
 539 │     )
 540 │ 
 541 │     return (
 542 │         list(itertools.chain(*left_split)),
 543 │         list(itertools.chain(*right_split)),
 544 │     )
